tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

schema.name: ScheduleWakeup
schema.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# PR #2549 out-of-scope follow-ups

Deferred from the 2026-10-14 review of fix-claude-review-stream-parser (head c512ab12d).

- Contract `verdict` field: add `"verdict":"approve|approve_with_nits|request_changes"` to the trail JSON line and check it against the comment count, replacing the keyword list in `proseReportsFindings` (trail_report.go).
- Worker token cost: workers get the JSON instruction even when a judge runs (cmd.go:1349). It is only read if synthesis fails; decide whether that fallback is worth the tokens.
- TUI rebuild cost: `refreshDetailContent` rebuilds the whole detail buffer on every streamed event (tui_model.go:362). Predates this PR; this PR adds a per-block `stripTrailJSON`.
- Display stripping outside trail mode: `stripTrailJSON` also runs in local mode and the judge prompt, hiding a reviewer's trailing quoted JSON with a `summary`/`comments` key. Unlikely; only strip when the run asked for the contract.

fix(review): don't post clean verdicts as Trail findings

Trail: https://entire.io/gh/MuskanPaliwal/cli/trails/12

When a reviewer approves a change with nothing to report, `entire review` posts that approval to the Trail as a finding. The Trail then shows an "Unspecified finding" for a review that found nothing.

`reviewTrailFindingInputs` looked for a runner-style JSON last line or Markdown finding bullets in the reviewer output. A clean approval such as

```text
approve - no actionable findings
```

has neither, so the fallback posted the whole output as one severity-less, whole-change comment.

This originally surfaced alongside a Claude stream parsing bug that made Codex the only successful reviewer. #2699 has since fixed the parser. The clean-verdict behavior is independent of it and still reproduces with any reviewer that returns a plain approval.

## What changed

Trail mode now asks for findings in a machine-readable form instead of interpreting verdict prose.

When `output` is `trail`, the reviewer and judge prompts end with a required JSON line:

```json
{"summary":"one-sentence verdict","comments":[{"severity":"high","body":"bug; impact; fix","location":{"granularity":"line","file_path":"path/to/file.go","start_line":42}}]}
```

The instruction is appended after profile and per-run text so neither can displace it, and it is skipped for a verbatim `prompt` override. The Markdown report stays as it was; the line is extra. Local runs do not ask for it.

Posting reads that line (`trail_report.go`):

- `"comments":[]` posts nothing and prints the existing "Nothing to report" notice, unless the prose contradicts it: a list item (including `•`), a severity marker (including a `### High` heading or `**High**`), a feedback label such as `Nits:` or `Findings:` at any indentation, or a non-approving verdict such as `request changes`, `approve with nits`, or `needs changes`, with or without a `Verdict:` label. Then the prose is posted as before.
- Comments post as native findings with their severity and location (line, range, file, or whole change). Entries without a body are dropped. If the prose has more severity-marked findings than the line has comments, the line is incomplete and the prose is posted instead. The prose normally repeats every comment, so posting both would duplicate them.
- When a judge runs, its line alone decides what is posted. The judge is asked to drop unsupported claims, so a reviewer's comment does not bypass it.
- Without a judge, each reviewer's report is read separately and the comments are merged. The report is the last stretch of text between tool calls that ends with a valid line, found by that line rather than by position, so a trailing tool call does not hide it. Earlier narration such as "I'll check the changed files:" followed by a bulleted file list cannot contradict a clean report. When the report does contradict its line, that report is posted; a reviewer with no valid line posts its whole narrative, as before.
- A missing or malformed line (no `comments` array) posts the prose with any trailing JSON removed, split into findings by top-level bullet. This is the previous behavior, so custom judge prompts that ignore the contract keep working. A JSON-only reply posts its `summary` rather than raw JSON. When nothing readable is left, nothing is posted and the run says the review produced no readable report.

When unsure, it posts. A false "clean" would hide a real finding, while a false "not clean" only restores the previous behavior.

The posting check and the bridge's prose splitter share one severity-marker and list-item detector, so prose judged to have findings also splits into them.

The JSON line is kept in the saved manifest and hidden from reviewer dumps, the rendered judge verdict, the live TUI detail view, and the `entire review --findings` list and detail views.

`Deps.PostReviewToTrail` now takes a `TrailReport` (structured comments or prose, never both). The bridge maps comments straight to Trail finding inputs and drops its own last-line JSON parsing.

Streamed reviewer output needed one supporting change. `AssistantText` gains a `Delta` flag that marks a fragment continuing the previous text of the same message. Pi sets it for `message_update` fragments and resets at `message_end`, and `joinAssistantText` joins such fragments without a separator, so a JSON line split across fragments is still one line.

Earlier commits on this branch classified verdict prose with heuristics. The contract replaces that. What remains is a fail-open check that only decides whether the prose contradicts an empty or incomplete comments array.

## Tests

- `review/trail_report_test.go`: judge JSON with empty, structured, fenced, pretty-printed, `null`, missing, and bodiless comments; a JSON-only reply with `null` comments posting its summary, and one with nothing readable not reaching the hook; empty JSON contradicted by a bullet, an indented or unicode bullet, a feedback label, a severity heading or bold marker, or a non-clean verdict, and not contradicted by a labeled approve, a word that merely starts with a marker, or a bold word after one; comments missing a severity-marked prose finding posting the prose; the judge deciding over a reviewer's high-severity comment; single and multiple reviewers without a judge, including one reviewer without JSON; narration bullets before a tool call not contradicting a clean report, while a finding bullet in the report posts only that report, not the narration or text after a trailing tool call; streamed deltas joining into one parsable line and a new message starting a new line after a tool call; the instruction's own example line parsing; JSON stripped for display and from the `--findings` preview.
- `review/prompt_test.go` and `review/synthesis_prompt_test.go`: the contract is appended last in trail mode and absent otherwise.
- `review/posttrail_test.go`: posting, skipping, and error paths through `maybePostReviewToTrail` with the new report type.
- `review_bridge_test.go`: structured comments map to finding inputs; unicode bullets and bold severity lines split into separate findings; a whole-change prose verdict still posts as one `verdict`-kind finding.
- `agent/pi/reviewer_test.go`: text deltas carry the `Delta` flag only when continuing a message.

## Scope

This does not change reviewer failure policy, Trail API types, or server rendering. Prompts change only in trail mode.

I found it. It isn't in the working tree. It sits in the worktree's git directory, `.bare/worktrees/fix-claude-review-stream-parser/OUT_OF_SCOPE.md`. It lists 4 deferred items from the review of PR #2549 at `c512ab12d`. I checked each against the PR's goal: stop posting clean approvals as Trail findings by having the reviewer end with a JSON line. I also checked them against the current code at `169b89af2`.

| # | Item | Out of scope? | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Add a `verdict` field to the JSON line and drop the keyword list in `proseReportsFindings` | **Yes** | This would change the contract that every prompt and parser uses, so it's new design work. The keyword list (`trail_report.go:236`) only fails one way: if it misses a keyword, it posts the prose, which is the old behavior. It can't hide a finding, so leaving it is safe. |
| 2 | Reviewers get the JSON instruction even when a judge runs (`cmd.go:1349`) | **Yes, but keep the current behavior** | A run with several reviewers always has a judge (`cmd.go:1035`), so every reviewer pays for the instruction. Their JSON is only read when the judge produces nothing (`trail_report.go:57-77`). Without the instruction, that fallback would post clean approvals as findings again, which is the original bug. I'd keep it rather than "decide later". |
| 3 | The TUI rebuilds the whole detail view on every streamed event (`tui_model.go:362`) | **Yes** | This was true before the PR. The PR only adds a per-block `stripTrailJSON` inside the existing rebuild (`tui_detail.go:70`), so it adds a little cost per event but doesn't change how often the view is rebuilt. |
| 4 | JSON is hidden from display even outside trail mode | **Borderline. This PR introduces it.** | `stripTrailJSON` runs everywhere without checking the mode: `synthesis_sink.go:160`, `tui_detail.go:70`, `dump.go:77,82`, `fix.go:208,242,246`, `synthesis_prompt.go:67`. Before this PR, local mode showed reviewer output as-is. It's still unlikely to matter: a reviewer's reply would have to end with a JSON block that has a valid `comments` array. The file's wording ("a `summary`/`comments` key") is broader than the code (`trail_report.go:186, 210-214`). |

**Bottom line:** items 1–3 are correctly deferred. Item 4 is a small regression this PR introduces, not old behavior, so a reviewer could fairly ask for it here. You could fix it by only hiding the line when the run asked for it, which means passing the mode to about 8 places. Or you could keep deferring it and say so in the PR's Scope section, which currently doesn't mention it.

Do you want me to draft that Scope line, or plan the item 4 fix?

content.text:
Here's the proposal for item 4 and the draft PR comment for items 1–3. I haven't edited or posted anything yet.

## Pre-edit brief: item 4

**Problem:** `entire review` now hides a reviewer's trailing JSON block even in local mode, where nobody asked for one. Suppose a local reviewer ends with an example payload like `{"summary":"…","comments":[…]}`, say while reviewing this very feature. That block disappears from the terminal output, the judge's input, the TUI detail view, and `--findings`. Before this PR, local output was shown as-is.

**Root cause:** `stripTrailJSON` (`trail_report.go:210`) decides from the text alone. It never checks whether the run asked for the JSON line. It's called in 8 places, and only the judge-related ones know the run's mode:

| Call site | Does it know the mode? |
|---|---|
| `synthesis_sink.go:160` (judge output shown to the user) | Yes, `s.TrailFindingsJSON` |
| `synthesis_prompt.go:67` (reviewer reports passed to the judge) | Yes, `opts.trailFindingsJSON` |
| `dump.go:77,82` (`DumpSink`) | No |
| `tui_detail.go:70` (TUI detail view) | No |
| `fix.go:208,242,246` (`--findings`, read from the saved manifest) | No, and the manifest doesn't record the mode |

**Proposed change:** add a `trailFindingsJSON bool` parameter to `stripTrailJSON` and pass the run's mode down to each call site:
- `DumpSink` gets a `TrailFindingsJSON` field. It's set in `composeMultiAgentSinks` and `composeSingleAgentSinks` (5 construction sites in `cmd.go`).
- `NewTUISink` and `newReviewTUIModel` take the flag, and `buildEventLines` passes it along.
- `LocalReviewManifest` gets `TrailFindingsJSON bool \`json:"trail_findings_json,omitempty"\``, set when the manifest is built, and `fix.go` reads it. Manifests saved before this change have no such field, so their output is shown unchanged. That's correct, because those runs predate the JSON line.
- The Trail posting path (`splitTrailJSON` in `trailReportFor`) doesn't change.

**Tests (written first, per your rule):** the existing tests that check the JSON is hidden in the display and `--findings` preview will pass the flag explicitly. New cases will check that local mode keeps a trailing contract-shaped JSON block visible in `DumpSink`, the TUI detail lines, the judge prompt, the judge display, and `--findings`. Then I'll run `mise run check`.

**Tradeoffs:** the plumbing touches about 6 files. A smaller fix, matching on content more narrowly, can't tell local from trail mode, so it wouldn't fix the cause. The manifest gains one optional field.

## Draft PR comment (items 1–3)

> Follow-ups I'm deliberately leaving out of this PR:
>
> - **A `verdict` field in the JSON line.** Adding `"verdict":"approve|approve_with_nits|request_changes"` and checking it against the comment count could replace the keyword list in `proseReportsFindings`. It changes the contract every prompt and parser shares, so it deserves its own change. The keyword list only fails toward posting, so it can't hide a finding in the meantime.
> - **Reviewers get the JSON instruction even when a judge runs.** Their line is only read if the judge produces nothing. I'm keeping it: without it, a failed judge falls back to reviewer prose, and a clean approval would be posted as a finding again. Whether that fallback is worth the extra tokens can be decided separately.
> - **TUI detail rebuild cost.** `refreshDetailContent` rebuilds the whole detail view on every streamed event. That predates this PR, which only adds a per-block strip inside the existing rebuild.

Can I go ahead with the item 4 change as described? And is the comment text OK to post on #2549 as is? I'll post it only after you approve it, and after item 4 is pushed if you'd rather it go up together.

Follow-up, out of scope for this PR.

While reworking trail posting around the JSON line, a design review found four gaps in how agent findings reach the trail. All four already exist on `main`, in both the Markdown fallback and the old JSON parser. I'm leaving them out so this PR stays about one thing, which is not posting clean reviews.

1. The model picks `file_path`, `start_line` and `end_line`, and the CLI reads those lines from the worktree and uploads them with the finding. The read can't leave the worktree, but it can reach untracked or ignored files like `.env`, and nothing caps `end_line`. This is the one I'd fix first. Reads should stay within files in the reviewed diff, with a capped span.
2. The CLI posts the model's `selected_text` as is, so a finding can pin made-up text to a real `file:line`. It should come from the worktree read, or get dropped when it doesn't match.
3. Nothing limits comment count or body length before the API call.
4. The judge prompt fences each reviewer report with fixed BEGIN/END markers, so a reviewer's output can close its own fence. Random per-run markers would stop that.

I'll pick these up in a follow-up PR.

Follow-up, out of scope for this PR.

While reworking trail posting around the JSON line, a design review found four gaps in how agent findings reach the trail. All four already exist on `main`, in both the Markdown fallback and the old JSON parser. I'm leaving them out so this PR stays about one thing, which is not posting clean reviews.

1. The model picks `file_path`, `start_line` and `end_line`, and the CLI reads those lines from the worktree and uploads them with the finding. The read can't leave the worktree, but it can reach untracked or ignored files like `.env`, and nothing caps `end_line`. This is the one I'd fix first. Reads should stay within files in the reviewed diff, with a capped span.
2. The CLI posts the model's `selected_text` as is, so a finding can pin made-up text to a real `file:line`. It should come from the worktree read, or get dropped when it doesn't match.
3. Nothing limits comment count or body length before the API call.
4. The judge prompt fences each reviewer report with fixed BEGIN/END markers, so a reviewer's output can close its own fence. Random per-run markers would stop that.

A later review of this branch turned up three more I'm also leaving out:

5. A `verdict` field in the JSON line (`approve`, `approve_with_nits`, `request_changes`), checked against the comment count, could replace the keyword list in `proseReportsFindings`. It changes the contract every prompt and parser shares, so it deserves its own change. The keyword list only fails toward posting, so it can't hide a finding in the meantime.
6. Reviewers get the JSON instruction even when a judge runs, and their line is only read if the judge produces nothing. I'm keeping it for now: without it, a failed judge falls back to reviewer prose, and a clean approval would be posted as a finding again. Whether that fallback is worth the tokens can be decided separately.
7. `refreshDetailContent` rebuilds the TUI detail view on every streamed event. That predates this PR, which only adds a per-block strip inside the existing rebuild.

I'll pick these up in a follow-up PR.
EOF

1	// Package review — see env.go for package-level rationale.
2	//
3	// tui_detail.go provides the alt-screen drill-in renderer. The body content is
4	// produced by [eventLines] (one or more wrapped lines per event) and fed into
5	// a bubbles/v2/viewport on [reviewTUIModel]; this file's [detailFrame] is the
6	// pure-function chrome (header + body + footer) that wraps the viewport's
7	// pre-rendered output and pads to exactly termHeight lines so every frame has
8	// the same line count (avoids ghost rows in Bubble Tea's alt-screen diff).
9	package review

12		"fmt"

14

16	)
17	
18	// eventLines converts a single Event to one or more display lines for the
19	// detail view, wrapped to maxWidth display cells. AssistantText preserves
20	// embedded '\n' as paragraph breaks; other event types render as a single
21	// sanitized line that wraps only on width overflow.
22	func eventLines(ev reviewtypes.Event, maxWidth int) []string {
23		if maxWidth <= 0 {
24			return nil
25		}
26		var raw string
27		switch e := ev.(type) {
28		case reviewtypes.Started:
29			raw = "[started]"
30		case reviewtypes.AssistantText:
31			// AssistantText is the only event that can contain meaningful
32			// multi-line content; wrapDisplayWidth honors embedded newlines.
33			return wrapDisplayWidth(e.Text, maxWidth)
34		case reviewtypes.ToolCall:
35			raw = fmt.Sprintf("[tool: %s] %s", e.Name, e.Args)
36		case reviewtypes.Tokens:
37			raw = fmt.Sprintf("[tokens in=%d out=%d]", e.In, e.Out)
38		case reviewtypes.Finished:
39			if e.Success {
40				raw = "[finished: success]"
41			} else {
42				raw = "[finished: failed]"
43			}
44		case reviewtypes.RunError:
45			if e.Err != nil {
46				raw = fmt.Sprintf("[error: %v]", e.Err)
47			} else {
48				raw = "[error]"
49			}
50		default:
51			raw = "[unknown event]"
52		}
53	
54		return wrapDisplayWidth(raw, maxWidth)
55	}

content.content:
1	# General Review Lessons
2	
3	- Make a guard's zero-match check count only the matches it is meant to protect. Matches that are always present, like the guard's own allowed cases, keep the check from ever firing.
4	- Test a guard by planting a violation and by breaking its detection, and see it fail both times. A guard that passes on clean code proves nothing.
5	- Before acting on a review finding, check whether existing tests or contracts explain the current shape. A structural test can be why the code looks the way it does.
6	- When code reads a user-owned config into a typed struct and writes it back, keep the fields it does not model. Any new reason to rewrite the file otherwise silently deletes user data.
7	- Make a new outer timeout longer than every internal budget on that path. Otherwise the kill fires before the code's own graceful fallback.
8	- Before setting an explicit timeout, look up the platform's current default for that exact event; an explicit value can shorten the budget rather than add one.
9	- When splitting known from unknown JSON keys to preserve them, decode only the exact known keys and keep every other key, case variants included, as unknown. `encoding/json` matches field names case-insensitively, so decoding the whole object lets a key like `"Command"` overwrite the real field.
10	- When a change makes a fix command riskier or changes which command to run, update every place that tells the user to run it (status, doctor, help text). Otherwise one screen sends people to the safe fix and the next to the destructive one.
11	- When a test plants a failure to cover an error branch, make sure an earlier step doesn't fail first; otherwise the assertion passes without ever running that branch.
12	- Select an agent's final report by a marker it carries (such as the contract line), not by its position in the event stream; a trailing tool call or an empty message ID moves a position-based boundary.

file.content:
# General Review Lessons

- Make a guard's zero-match check count only the matches it is meant to protect. Matches that are always present, like the guard's own allowed cases, keep the check from ever firing.
- Test a guard by planting a violation and by breaking its detection, and see it fail both times. A guard that passes on clean code proves nothing.
- Before acting on a review finding, check whether existing tests or contracts explain the current shape. A structural test can be why the code looks the way it does.
- When code reads a user-owned config into a typed struct and writes it back, keep the fields it does not model. Any new reason to rewrite the file otherwise silently deletes user data.
- Make a new outer timeout longer than every internal budget on that path. Otherwise the kill fires before the code's own graceful fallback.
- Before setting an explicit timeout, look up the platform's current default for that exact event; an explicit value can shorten the budget rather than add one.
- When splitting known from unknown JSON keys to preserve them, decode only the exact known keys and keep every other key, case variants included, as unknown. `encoding/json` matches field names case-insensitively, so decoding the whole object lets a key like `"Command"` overwrite the real field.
- When a change makes a fix command riskier or changes which command to run, update every place that tells the user to run it (status, doctor, help text). Otherwise one screen sends people to the safe fix and the next to the destructive one.
- When a test plants a failure to cover an error branch, make sure an earlier step doesn't fail first; otherwise the assertion passes without ever running that branch.
- Select an agent's final report by a marker it carries (such as the contract line), not by its position in the event stream; a trailing tool call or an empty message ID moves a position-based boundary.

input.content:
Follow-up, out of scope for this PR.

While reworking trail posting around the JSON line, a design review found four gaps in how agent findings reach the trail. All four already exist on `main`, in both the Markdown fallback and the old JSON parser. I'm leaving them out so this PR stays about one thing, which is not posting clean reviews.

1. The model picks `file_path`, `start_line` and `end_line`, and the CLI reads those lines from the worktree and uploads them with the finding. The read can't leave the worktree, but it can reach untracked or ignored files like `.env`, and nothing caps `end_line`. This is the one I'd fix first. Reads should stay within files in the reviewed diff, with a capped span.
2. The CLI posts the model's `selected_text` as is, so a finding can pin made-up text to a real `file:line`. It should come from the worktree read, or get dropped when it doesn't match.
3. Nothing limits comment count or body length before the API call.
4. The judge prompt fences each reviewer report with fixed BEGIN/END markers, so a reviewer's output can close its own fence. Random per-run markers would stop that.

A later review of this branch turned up three more I'm also leaving out:

5. A `verdict` field in the JSON line (`approve`, `approve_with_nits`, `request_changes`), checked against the comment count, could replace the keyword list in `proseReportsFindings`. It changes the contract every prompt and parser shares, so it deserves its own change. The keyword list only fails toward posting, so it can't hide a finding in the meantime.
6. Reviewers get the JSON instruction even when a judge runs, and their line is only read if the judge produces nothing. I'm keeping it for now: without it, a failed judge falls back to reviewer prose, and a clean approval would be posted as a finding again. Whether that fallback is worth the tokens can be decided separately.
7. `refreshDetailContent` rebuilds the TUI detail view on every streamed event. That predates this PR, which only adds a per-block strip inside the existing rebuild.

I'll pick these up in a follow-up PR.

5. A `verdict` field in the JSON line (`approve`, `approve_with_nits`, `request_changes`), checked against the comment count, could replace the keyword list in `proseReportsFindings`. It changes the contract every prompt and parser shares, so it deserves its own change. The keyword list only fails toward posting, so it can't hide a finding in the meantime.
6. Reviewers get the JSON instruction even when a judge runs, and their line is only read if the judge produces nothing. I'm keeping it for now: without it, a failed judge falls back to reviewer prose, and a clean approval would be posted as a finding again. Whether that fallback is worth the tokens can be decided separately.
7. `refreshDetailContent` rebuilds the TUI detail view on every streamed event. That predates this PR, which only adds a per-block strip inside the existing rebuild.

I'll pick these up in a follow-up PR.

The PR comment edit didn't go through: Claude Code's auto-mode permission check blocked it as a write to an external system. It's ready for you to run.

**The fix:** `stripTrailJSON` now takes the run's mode and leaves the text alone unless the run asked for the JSON line. The mode is passed to every place that hides it:
- the post-run output (`DumpSink`);
- the TUI detail view (`NewTUISink` takes the mode, and so does `buildEventLines`);
- the judge prompt and the judge's displayed verdict;
- `--findings`, which reads a new `trail_findings_json` field saved in the manifest. Manifests saved before this change don't have the field, so their output is shown unchanged. That's correct, because those runs predate the JSON line.

Posting to the Trail is unchanged.

**Verification:**
- **New test:** I wrote `TestTrailJSONHiddenOnlyWhenRequested` before the fix. It checks all 6 places in both modes: a trail run hides the line and keeps the prose, and a local run keeps the line.
- **It catches the bug:** I temporarily removed the mode check, and all 6 places failed. I then restored the code.
- **Existing tests:** the judge-prompt test in `synthesis_prompt_test.go` used the local-mode helper to check hiding, so I switched it to the trail-mode one. The other test edits only add the new argument.

- **Not tested:** the one line in `writePostReviewManifest` that saves the mode in the manifest. Testing it needs real session state, and the existing tests for that function stop before a manifest is saved.
